task1.title: Reasons for UK university study
task1.prompt: The charts below show the reasons of students to study a particular in a UK university in the year 1987 and 2007.

chartDesc.title: Reasons why students chose a college or university, UK
chartDesc.overview: In both 1987 and 2007, suitable degree courses remained the most popular reason for choosing a university in the UK. Over the 20-year period, selection based on close proximity to parental home more than doubled, while decision-making based on good sports and social activities fell significantly.
keyFeatures: From the 1987 chart, suitable degree courses was the highest category at 35%, followed by quality of resources at 21% and good sports and social activities at 19%.
From the 1987 chart, quality teaching and close to parental home were the lowest reasons at 15% and 10% respectively.
From the 2007 chart, suitable degree courses remained the top choice, rising slightly to 37%.
From the 2007 chart, close to parental home increased substantially from 10% in 1987 to 22% in 2007, making it the second most common reason.
From the 2007 chart, good sports and social activities dropped sharply from 19% in 1987 down to 6% in 2007, becoming the least common reason.
From both charts, quality of resources fell from 21% in 1987 to 17% in 2007, whereas quality teaching rose slightly from 15% to 18%.

task1.instruction: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparison where relevant.
task1.sampleBand5:
The pie charts show the reasons why students study in UK universities in 1987 and 2007. It shows different reasons for their choices.

In 1987, the main reason was job opportunities, at 40%. Course content was also important, with 25%. Career prospects was 15% and reputation of the university was 10%. Other reasons were only 10%. The year 2007 was different.

In 2007, the biggest reason was still job opportunities, but it decreased to 30%. Course content was the same, 25%. But the reputation of the university increased a lot, to 20%. Career prospects were 15%, same as before. Other reasons increased to 10%. This shows that university reputation became more important, and job opportunities became a little less important over the 20 years.
task1.sampleBand6:
The pie charts give information about the reasons why students chose to study at UK universities in 1987 and 2007. Overall, career opportunities were the main reason in both years, but other reasons changed.

In 1987, the most popular reason was career prospects at 34%. The second biggest reason was interest in the subject, which accounted for 22%. Advice from teachers and family made up 18% of the reasons. The remaining reasons, better salary and other reasons, made up 13% each.

By 2007, career prospects had increased to 40%. Interest in subject dropped to 15%. However, salary increased to 20%, showing a shift in priorities. Advice from teachers and family decreased to 10%. The 'other' reasons category saw a significant increase to 15% which could suggest new factors influencing student choices in 2007.
task1.sampleBand7:
The pie charts illustrate the primary reasons why students chose to study at UK universities in 1987 and 2007. Overall, career prospects were the dominant motivation in both years, although its significance increased, while the influence of other factors generally declined.

In 1987, the largest proportion of students, 33%, were driven by career prospects. This was followed by an interest in the subject, accounting for 27% of responses. The university's reputation was the next most important factor at 18%, while better qualifications and other reasons made up 12% and 10% respectively.

By 2007, the proportion of students citing career prospects as their main reason had risen significantly to 45%. Interest in the subject remained a key motivator, but had decreased to 21%. Similarly, the university's reputation saw a drop to 15%. A notable decrease was observed in the percentage of students seeking better qualifications, which fell to 9%. Interestingly, other reasons remained relatively stable, accounting for 10% of the responses. It is evident that career prospects became an increasingly important factor over this period, while the others became less so.
task1.sampleBand8:
The charts illustrate the varying motivations behind students' choices of a particular degree at UK universities in 1987 and 2007. Overall, career prospects were the dominant factor in both years, although its significance shifted considerably. Furthermore, interest in the subject saw a decline, while the influence of advice from school teachers rose.

In 1987, career prospects constituted the primary driver, accounting for 45% of students' decisions. Interest in the subject followed at 34%, with advice from school teachers playing a relatively minor role at 12%. Influence from family and friends was the least significant reason, at only 9%. By 2007, the percentage of students citing career prospects as the reason for their choice had surged to 61%. Conversely, the proportion of students motivated by their interest in the subject had dwindled to 17%.

Interestingly, the influence of school teachers more than doubled, climbing to 25% in 2007. While still the least influential factor, family and friends saw a slight increase to 17%. In conclusion, while career aspirations remained paramount, the importance of subject interest decreased substantially, and the role of educational advisors became more pronounced over the two decades.
task1.sampleBand9:
The charts illustrate the primary motivations for students choosing a particular field of study at UK universities in 1987 and 2007. Overall, while career prospects and interest in the subject remained significant factors, the relative importance of each shifted considerably over the two decades.

In 1987, the paramount reason for selecting a specific course was career opportunities, cited by 45% of students. Interest in the subject followed closely at 38%, demonstrating a strong correlation between personal passion and vocational aims. Advice from teachers and family played a minor role, accounting for 10% and 7% respectively. By 2007, however, the landscape had altered. While career prospects remained important, their influence diminished to 33%. Interest in the subject gained considerable ground, becoming the most significant factor at 40%.

A noteworthy shift occurred in the influence of external advisors. Teacher influence experienced a marked decline, falling to a mere 5%. Conversely, family advice saw a modest increase to 12%. This suggests a possible change in the perceived value of different sources of guidance. In summary, the key driver for course selection evolved from primarily career-focused to more intrinsically motivated by 2007, with the role of teachers waning and families gaining slightly in influence. The data underscores a shifting paradigm in student priorities. The trends are quite divergent. It can be clearly seen that interest in the topic became more pronounced over the period.
task1.sampleAnswer:
The bar charts compare the primary motivations for students enrolling at a specific UK university in 1987 and 2007. Overall, it is evident that while interest in the subject remained the dominant factor in both years, there was a significant shift toward employment-related motivations by 2007. Conversely, more personal or social reasons for studying saw a decline in popularity over the twenty-year period.

In 1987, 'Interest in the subject' was the single most cited reason, with nearly 45% of students choosing this option. By 2007, this figure dropped slightly to approximately 40%, yet it remained the most prevalent motivation. In contrast, 'Career prospects' saw a substantial increase, rising from just under 20% in 1987 to nearly 35% in 2007, highlighting a growing focus on the professional utility of higher education.

Other motivations such as 'Parental pressure' and 'Social life' experienced a downward trend. Parental influence fell from 15% to a mere 5%, while the desire for a social life as a primary driver decreased from 10% to around 7%. Interestingly, 'Lack of other options' emerged as a more significant factor in 2007, doubling from 5% to 10%. This suggests that for a tenth of the student body, university had become a default choice rather than a proactive pursuit.

task2.title: Unemployment vs unsatisfying jobs
task2.prompt: It is better for people to be unemployed than people to be employed but they do not enjoy. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
task2.instruction: To what extent do you agree or disagree?
task2.sampleBand5:
Some people think that it is not good to work if you do not like the job. I think this is true to some extent, but it is also important to have a job for money and other things.

If you are unemployed, you might be happier because you are not doing something you hate. You can spend your time doing things you enjoy, like hobbies or seeing friends. But, if you have no job, you will not have money. This can cause stress and problems. You need money for food, rent, and other important things. So, being unemployed can be hard.

On the other hand, if you are employed but do not like your job, you will have money. This is a good thing, but you might be unhappy. You might feel stressed and tired all the time. This can affect your health and your relationships. Some people think it is better to be poor and happy than rich and sad. But, it is also hard to be poor.

It is important to try and find a job that you enjoy. This is not always easy, but it is worth trying. If you cannot find a job you love, you can try to find a job that you do not hate. Or, you can try to make your job better by talking to your boss or finding new challenges.

In conclusion, I think it is better to be employed, even if you do not enjoy the job. This is because you need money to live. But, it is also important to try and find a job that makes you happy. I hope one day everyone can find a job they like.
task2.sampleBand6:
Some people believe that it is preferable to be unemployed than to have a job that you dislike. While I understand the reasons for this view, I mostly disagree. I think being employed, even if the job isn't perfect, is generally better.

On the one hand, being unemployed can have its advantages. If someone hates their job, it can cause a lot of stress and unhappiness. This can affect their health and relationships. Therefore, it might seem better to be unemployed and look for something more suitable. Furthermore, unemployment can provide an opportunity to retrain or start a business. This can lead to a more fulfilling career in the long run, even if it takes some time.

However, I think there are more benefits to being employed, even in a job you don't love. Firstly, a job provides financial security. This is very important for paying bills and supporting yourself and your family. Unemployment can cause financial hardship and stress. Secondly, work provides a sense of purpose and routine. This can be important for mental health. Even if the job is boring, it can still give you a reason to get up in the morning and be productive. Thirdly, being employed can open doors to new opportunities. You can learn new skills, meet new people, and gain experience that can help you find a better job later on.

In conclusion, while I understand that being in a job you hate can be difficult, I believe that the benefits of employment, such as financial security and a sense of purpose, outweigh the negatives. Therefore, I think it is generally better to be employed than unemployed, even if the job is not ideal. People can always actively seek a more satisfying position while employed.
task2.sampleBand7:
The question of whether it is preferable to be unemployed rather than employed in an unfulfilling job is a complex one. While both situations present challenges, I believe that unemployment is generally the less desirable option, although I recognise that there are circumstances where a dissatisfying job can take a significant toll on an individual's well-being.

One of the primary reasons I disagree with the statement is the financial strain that unemployment places on individuals and families. Without a steady income, people may struggle to afford basic necessities such as housing, food, and healthcare. This can lead to significant stress and anxiety, potentially impacting their mental and physical health. While a job one dislikes is not ideal, it at least provides financial security and the ability to meet essential needs. Furthermore, even a job that is not inherently enjoyable can offer opportunities for skill development and networking, which can be beneficial in the long run.

However, I acknowledge that there are situations where the negative impacts of a dissatisfying job outweigh the benefits of employment. If a job is extremely stressful, toxic, or morally objectionable, it can have a detrimental effect on a person's mental and emotional well-being. In such cases, it may be justifiable to leave the job, even without another one lined up. This is because prolonged exposure to such an environment can lead to burnout, depression, and other serious health problems. It is crucial, however, to have a plan in place to address the financial challenges of unemployment, such as seeking government assistance or exploring alternative income streams.

Moreover, it is important to consider the individual's personality and values. Some people are more resilient and better able to cope with a dissatisfying job than others. Others may find it easier to tolerate a job they dislike if it allows them to pursue their passions and interests outside of work. Ultimately, the decision of whether to remain in an unfulfilling job or to become unemployed is a personal one that depends on a variety of factors. There is no one-size-fits-all answer.

In conclusion, while I appreciate that there are downsides to being employed in a job that one does not enjoy, I believe that the financial and practical benefits of employment generally outweigh the drawbacks. However, it is important to recognise that there are circumstances where the negative impacts of a dissatisfying job can be so severe that unemployment becomes the preferable option. A carefully considered approach is needed in each individual case.
task2.sampleBand8:
The question of whether unemployment is preferable to unfulfilling employment is a complex one, sparking considerable debate. While the financial hardships associated with joblessness cannot be ignored, I firmly believe that being unemployed is, in many respects, a better alternative than remaining in a job that brings no satisfaction. This is because prolonged unhappiness at work can have detrimental effects on mental and physical well-being, and unemployment can provide opportunities for personal growth and career re-evaluation.

Firstly, enduring a job one dislikes can significantly impact an individual's mental and physical health. The constant stress and lack of fulfillment can lead to anxiety, depression, and even burnout. This, in turn, can manifest in physical ailments such as insomnia, digestive problems, and a weakened immune system. For instance, a friend of mine worked for years in a high-pressure sales job that he found deeply unsatisfying. The resulting stress led to chronic migraines and ultimately forced him to take a leave of absence. In contrast, unemployment, while stressful in its own way, can offer a chance to recuperate and prioritize self-care, potentially leading to improved overall health.

Secondly, unemployment can serve as a catalyst for positive change and personal development. While the initial period may be challenging, it can also provide a valuable opportunity to reassess one's career goals and explore new avenues. Individuals can use this time to acquire new skills, pursue further education, or even start their own businesses. For example, someone who loses their job in a declining industry might use the opportunity to retrain in a field with better prospects, such as technology or renewable energy. Furthermore, unemployment can free up time for pursuing personal interests and hobbies, which can boost self-esteem and provide a sense of purpose. Such experiences can be profoundly transformative, leading to a more fulfilling and meaningful life.

Of course, the financial difficulties associated with unemployment are undeniable, and governments and individuals must actively seek solutions to mitigate these challenges. However, the long-term consequences of remaining in a soul-crushing job can be equally, if not more, damaging. Therefore, while acknowledging the hardships of unemployment, I maintain that it is ultimately preferable to being trapped in a job that offers no personal satisfaction or sense of purpose. It provides a chance for recovery, reflection, and the pursuit of a more fulfilling career path, something which an unfulfilling job rarely, if ever, allows. The potential for personal and professional reinvention makes unemployment, in this context, a more advantageous position.

In conclusion, although the financial burden of being unemployed is a significant concern, the potential for improved mental and physical health, coupled with opportunities for personal and professional growth, make unemployment a more desirable option than remaining in a job that actively diminishes one's well-being. This perspective acknowledges the inherent value of individual happiness and fulfillment in the context of work.
task2.sampleBand9:
The assertion that unemployment is preferable to engaging in unfulfilling employment is a nuanced one, demanding careful consideration. While the detrimental psychological effects of a dissatisfying job cannot be ignored, I contend that, on balance, being employed, even in an unenjoyable role, generally offers more advantages than being unemployed. This essay will explore both perspectives before articulating my position.

On the one hand, the argument for unemployment being the lesser of two evils hinges on the profound impact of job dissatisfaction on mental well-being. Spending a significant portion of one's life in a role that inspires little to no enthusiasm can lead to chronic stress, anxiety, and even depression. This, in turn, can negatively affect personal relationships, physical health, and overall quality of life. Furthermore, an individual trapped in an unfulfilling job may experience a sense of stagnation, hindering personal growth and preventing them from pursuing more meaningful opportunities. The psychological toll can be so substantial that unemployment, with its potential for introspection, retraining, and a renewed sense of purpose, may indeed seem like a more attractive option.

However, the benefits of even an unfulfilling job should not be dismissed. Firstly, employment provides financial security, enabling individuals to meet their basic needs and support their families. This is particularly crucial in societies where social safety nets are weak or nonexistent. Secondly, employment offers a sense of structure and routine, which can be beneficial for mental health, providing a sense of purpose and social interaction. Even in a less-than-ideal role, individuals can develop valuable skills, build professional networks, and gain experience that enhances their future employability. Moreover, the financial stability afforded by employment allows individuals to pursue personal interests and hobbies outside of work, providing a much-needed sense of fulfillment and balance. Finally, it stands to reason that an individual can actively seek better employment opportunities while currently employed, a much easier task than job searching while unemployed.

In conclusion, while I acknowledge the detrimental effects of unfulfilling employment on mental well-being, I firmly believe that the benefits of being employed, even in a less-than-ideal role, generally outweigh the advantages of unemployment. The financial security, structure, skill development, and opportunities for personal growth and future advancement that employment provides are simply too significant to ignore. Therefore, it is my considered opinion that while striving for fulfilling employment is undoubtedly a worthwhile goal, being employed, even if unenjoyable, is generally the more advantageous position. This perspective is not to diminish the importance of prioritising mental well-being, but rather to highlight the multifaceted benefits of employment beyond mere financial gain.
task2.sampleAnswer:
The question of whether an unsatisfactory job is preferable to having no job at all is a complex one, touching upon economic necessity and psychological well-being. While I acknowledge that chronic job dissatisfaction can lead to severe mental health issues, I largely disagree with the notion that unemployment is a better alternative, primarily due to the financial and social repercussions of being without work.

On the one hand, proponents of the idea that unemployment is better often point to the corrosive effects of a toxic work environment. Spending forty hours a week in a role that one loathes can lead to burnout, depression, and a diminished sense of self-worth. In such cases, the stress of the job may outweigh the salary earned, potentially damaging one's health and personal relationships. From a purely psychological standpoint, being free from a debilitating work environment allows an individual the mental space to recover and seek a more fulfilling career path.

However, the reality of unemployment is often far more grueling than a disliked job. Financial stability is the cornerstone of a functional life; without a steady income, individuals face the immediate stress of being unable to meet basic needs like housing and nutrition. Furthermore, a long-term gap in a CV can make future employment significantly harder to secure, creating a cycle of poverty and exclusion. Employment, even if unrewarding, provides a structured routine and a sense of social participation that is often lost when one is out of work. In most societies, a job also provides access to vital benefits such as healthcare and pension contributions.

In conclusion, while I agree that no one should remain in a miserable job indefinitely, I believe that being employed in an unenjoyable role is generally a more sustainable position than being unemployed. The practical and financial advantages of work typically provide a more secure foundation for eventually transitioning to a more satisfying career than the precarious state of unemployment ever could.
task2.uzSampleBand5:
Ba'zi odamlar, agar ish sizga yoqmasa, ishlash yaxshi emas deb hisoblashadi. Menimcha, bu ma'lum darajada to'g'ri, lekin pul va boshqa narsalar uchun ham ishga ega bo'lish muhimdir.

Agar siz ishsiz bo'lsangiz, siz yoqtirmaydigan ish bilan shug'ullanmaganingiz uchun baxtliroq bo'lishingiz mumkin. Siz vaqtingizni sevimli mashg'ulotlar yoki do'stlar bilan uchrashish kabi yoqtirgan ishlaringizga sarflashingiz mumkin. Ammo, agar sizda ish bo'lmasa, sizda pul bo'lmaydi. Bu stress va muammolarni keltirib chiqarishi mumkin. Sizga oziq-ovqat, ijara va boshqa muhim narsalar uchun pul kerak. Shunday qilib, ishsiz bo'lish qiyin bo'lishi mumkin.

Boshqa tomondan, agar siz ish bilan ta'minlangan bo'lsangiz, lekin ishingiz sizga yoqmasa, sizda pul bo'ladi. Bu yaxshi narsa, lekin siz baxtsiz bo'lishingiz mumkin. Siz doimo stressda va charchoq his qilishingiz mumkin. Bu sizning sog'lig'ingizga va munosabatlaringizga ta'sir qilishi mumkin. Ba'zi odamlar boy va qayg'uli bo'lgandan ko'ra, kambag'al va baxtli bo'lish yaxshiroq deb o'ylashadi. Lekin kambag'al bo'lish ham qiyin.

Sizga yoqadigan ishni topishga harakat qilish muhim. Bu har doim ham oson emas, lekin harakat qilishga arziydi. Agar siz sevimli ishingizni topa olmasangiz, siz yomon ko'rmaydigan ishni topishga harakat qilishingiz mumkin. Yoki, siz xo'jayiningiz bilan gaplashib yoki yangi qiyinchiliklarni topib, ishingizni yaxshilashga harakat qilishingiz mumkin.

Xulosa qilib aytganda, menimcha, hatto ish sizga yoqmasa ham, ish bilan ta'minlangan bo'lish yaxshiroqdir. Chunki siz yashash uchun pulga muhtojsiz. Lekin, sizni baxtli qiladigan ishni topishga harakat qilish ham muhim. Umid qilamanki, bir kun kelib hamma o'ziga yoqqan ishni topadi.
